title: Benchmark interpretation: Partial success can hide task failure
desc: Shows domain, grading, tools, hints and model versions alter results, supporting only bounded comparisons.

kps.k: Benchmark success depends on what a test measures; strong partial scores do not establish complete legal-task success.
kps.d: Vals Index reports that top models satisfy around 90% of criteria, yet achieve low task resolution under Harvey’s requirement that every criterion pass. By contrast, AI-MBE reports Claude 3.5 Sonnet answering 181 of 210 multiple-choice questions correctly. These findings measure different capabilities, not contradictory estimates of readiness for legal practice. Neither exam accuracy nor criterion-level performance alone establishes that users can rely directly on completed legal work.

qs.q: There is a clear trend: strong models and agents satisfy most criteria, around 90% for top models.

kps.k: Model rankings vary by domain and performance dimension rather than identifying a universally superior system.
kps.d: On XpertBench-Gold’s 245 tasks, Claude-Opus-4.6-thinking leads Law at 65.54%, narrowly ahead of Doubao-2.0-pro and GPT-5.4-high, while GPT-5.4-high leads Finance. JADE likewise separates final, reasoning, evidence and credibility scores: Gemini Deep Research leads the displayed research systems on final score, Shopping Research on evidence, and ChatGPT(Web Search) on credibility. These benchmark-specific rankings support task-specific comparisons, not a single cross-benchmark league table.

qs.q: Claude-Opus-4.6-thinking sets the benchmark in Law (65.54%) and Humanities (83.02%), whereas GPT-5.4-high demonstrates a commanding lead in Finance (84.65%), outperforming competitive models like Doubao-2.0-pro (73.82%).
qs.a: Xpertbench: Expert Level Tasks with Rubrics-Based Evaluation · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Automated grading infrastructure materially shapes the interpretation of results.
kps.d: Vals independently runs HLAB using Harvey’s protocol, with internet access disabled and GPT 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 as judges; the final score averages their task pass rates. Vals also reports fixing a document-reading bug so judges could see tracked insertions and deletions when grading redlines. These are model-judged benchmark findings, not human verification findings. The practical implication is to examine grading rules, judge configurations and document handling alongside headline scores.

qs.q: ## Methodology  We use Harvey’s generation and grading protocol in the same environment, with internet access disabled.

kps.k: More tool use, additional hints and newer model versions do not produce uniform gains.
kps.d: Vals observes that some models make substantially more search calls without higher accuracy. In “Graders should cheat,” GPT-4o’s win rate against Claude 3.5 Sonnet falls from 40.2% without hints to 26.6% with three, while Gemini 1.5 Flash’s rises from 42.2% to 47.0%. These relative win rates do not show that hints reduce absolute accuracy. XpertBench interprets some leading-model results as suggesting stronger formal-logic capabilities, but also reports GPT-5.2-high scoring below GPT-5-high in STEM. The tension concerns uneven capabilities and sensitivity to test conditions, rather than an explicit dispute between sources.

qs.q: Some models allocate effort more selectively: [Claude Opus 4.8](/models/anthropic_claude-opus-4-8) balances case-law and web search in roughly equal proportion, while others run many more total calls, especially web_search, without converting that into higher accuracy.
qs.a: Vals Index — Continuous Independent Agentic Benchmark (Legal Sector: Legal Research Bench + Independent HLAB Runs) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: The observation matches with what we have observed previously in Figure 4 where GPT-4o excels at solving hard problems while Gemini 1.5 Pro leverage hints well, which solves easier versions of those hard problems more effectively.
qs.a: Graders should cheat: privileged information enables expert-level automated evaluations · Academia · 2025

kps.k: The supplied evidence supports bounded comparisons, not conclusions about autonomous deployment or universal tool benefits.
kps.d: JADE reports means from three experimental runs, but its missing no-tool results prevent a with-versus-without-tools comparison. AI-MBE does not identify which of two listed Claude 3.5 Sonnet versions achieved the winning score. The supplied RubricEval, TheAgentCompany, Thai bar-essay and civil-legal-intake fragments lack sufficient labels or explanatory claims to support substantive conclusions. For practical assessment, distinguish test formats, model versions, scoring dimensions and complete-task pass rates; these excerpts do not establish deployment safety or quantify the human verification needed.

qs.q: All experiments were performed in triplicate, and the mean was reported.
qs.a: JADE: Expert-Grounded Dynamic Evaluation for Open-Ended Professional Tasks · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The selected legal-tech vendor sources accept the proposition that benchmark results support only bounded, task-specific comparisons. Their common basis is that headline performance varies with the capability measured, domain, model version and evaluation design. Collectively, they build on the proposition because Vals supplies a concrete methodological account of why strong criterion scores may coexist with low complete-task resolution and shows that document handling can materially affect automated grading. XpertBench reinforces the bounded-comparison argument through domain-specific leaders and uneven progress between model versions, but does not address complete legal-task success, grading reliability or deployment safety. Thus, the internal variation is complementary: Vals focuses on task-resolution rules and benchmark infrastructure, whereas XpertBench focuses on differences across domains and versions. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: The remaining gaps are large enough that task resolution stays low even when criterion-level performance looks strong.

vlens.an: The usable academia-and-research sources support the proposition that benchmark findings permit only bounded, task- and methodology-specific comparisons. They do so for complementary reasons: the hint study shows that changing test conditions alters models’ relative performance unevenly; AI-MBE reports a leader only on a defined multiple-choice bar-exam task and leaves ambiguity over the precise Claude 3.5 Sonnet version; and JADE separates final, reasoning, evidence and credibility scores, with different systems leading on different dimensions. Together, these findings caution against treating a strong partial score, a benchmark winner or a single ranking as proof of complete legal-task success, universal model superiority or deployment readiness. Material internal variation concerns evidential completeness rather than substantive disagreement: TheAgentCompany, the unlabelled model-results fragment, the Thai bar-essay study and RubricEval are unassessable because the supplied excerpts lack labels, methodology or explanatory claims. Their inclusion cannot be counted as support or opposition. This assessment describes only the curated sources supplied and does not establish how prevalent this view is across academia and research generally.

elens.an: Within the supplied Generative shock (2023–2024) material, the only substantively interpretable source supports the proposition that benchmark findings permit bounded, task- and methodology-specific comparisons. AI-MBE identifies a leading model on a narrowly defined test—210 multiple-choice MBE questions—but does not extend that result to complete legal-task performance, autonomous deployment or readiness for legal practice. Its excerpt also lists two Claude 3.5 Sonnet versions without identifying which produced the winning score, illustrating why model-version detail matters. Material internal variation lies chiefly in evidentiary completeness rather than disagreement: the two other records are truncated, unlabelled numerical fragments and therefore cannot be positioned. Their uncertainty does not amount to opposition or make the overall position Mixed. Because the corpus is curated, this assessment characterises only the supplied sources and does not imply broader prevalence.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition’s narrower methodological claim that benchmark results are conditional on test design and therefore warrant only bounded comparisons. Its hint-count results show that the same intervention changes relative performance differently across models: GPT models generally lose ground against Claude 3.5 Sonnet as more hints are supplied, whereas Gemini 1.5 Flash improves and Gemini 1.5 Pro peaks with two hints. The authors attribute this variation to differing strengths in solving intrinsically hard problems versus exploiting hints. This is evidence of sensitivity to benchmark conditions, not evidence that hints universally raise or lower absolute accuracy. The source does not itself address the synthesis’s broader claims about complete legal-task resolution, autonomous deployment, or required human verification, so its support is direct but limited to the hints-and-model-comparison component. Because only one curated source is supplied for this period, no inference about wider prevalence is warranted.

qs.q: The observation matches with what we have observed previously in Figure 4 where GPT-4o excels at solving hard problems while Gemini 1.5 Pro leverage hints well, which solves easier versions of those hard problems more effectively.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that benchmark results support only bounded, task-specific comparisons, and the strongest evidence materially develops it. Vals shows that high criterion-level performance can coexist with low complete-task resolution and demonstrates that grading rules, model-judge configurations and document-handling bugs can alter how results should be interpreted. XpertBench reinforces the proposition through domain-dependent leaders and a newer model underperforming its predecessor in STEM. JADE similarly reports different leaders across final, evidence and credibility dimensions, while its incomplete no-tool results prevent broader claims about tool benefits. Material internal variation concerns emphasis rather than direction: Vals addresses complete-task failure and benchmark infrastructure; XpertBench addresses domain and version variability; JADE addresses multidimensional scoring. The Thai bar-exam and RubricEval fragments are too incomplete to determine a position. These sources are a curated selection, so their alignment should not be treated as evidence of prevalence among 2026 researchers or evaluators.
